open-question.question: The side-bar view is a native VS Code tree listing every live mission, and each mission must show its title, the workflow step to run next, its count of open questions, its count of remaining tasks, and a marker while a run is going. A tree item offers a label, a description, a tooltip, an icon, and child rows. Which of these carries each of the five facts, and is a mission's row a leaf or does it expand into child rows?
open-question.alternative: A mission's row is a leaf with no child rows. The label carries the mission's title. The description carries the next workflow step's name followed by both counts in a compact form, for example "Derive tasks · 3 questions · 2 tasks". The icon carries the running marker: a spinning ThemeIcon while the mission's run is going and a steady mission icon otherwise. The tooltip repeats all five facts spelled out in full, beside the mission's path. Every fact the goal names is visible at a glance on one line per mission, using each TreeItem field for what VS Code draws it for. The list stays as long as the number of live missions, and the spinner is the editor's own idiom for work in progress. The description is the first text the editor truncates in a narrow side bar, so the counts, which come last, are the first to be cut off. The step name and two counts have to share one short dimmed string, which pushes toward abbreviations a person must learn.

A mission's row is a leaf with no child rows. The label carries the title. The icon carries the next workflow step as one ThemeIcon chosen per step (first review round, additional review round, derive tasks, execute tasks, finish), and while a run is going it is replaced by a spinning icon, which is how the running marker shows. The description carries only the two counts, for example "3 questions · 2 tasks". The tooltip names the step in words, the two counts, whether a run is going, and the path. The description stays short enough to survive a narrow side bar, and the step reads at a glance once its icons are known, which leaves the row's text for the counts. A person has to learn what each step's icon means, and until then needs the tooltip. While a run is going the spinner hides which step the mission is on. Choosing five or more codicons that read clearly as workflow steps is a design task of its own, and an icon on its own is not announced as a step name by a screen reader unless accessibility information is set.

A mission's row is a leaf with no child rows and no icon. The label carries the title. The description carries every other fact as text: a "running" word in front while a run is going, then the next step's name, then the two counts. The tooltip repeats the facts in full beside the path. Every fact is a word a person or a screen reader can read, with no icon meaning to learn, and the row needs no choice of codicons. The description is now holding four facts, so it truncates soonest of all the leaf layouts, and the running marker, which comes first, pushes the counts further toward the cut. A word is also much less noticeable than a spinner when scanning which missions are busy.

A mission's row is a leaf with no child rows. The label carries the title, the description carries only the next step's name, and the icon carries the running marker as a spinning icon while a run is going. The two counts appear only in the tooltip, beside the step, the running state, and the path. The row is the cleanest and least likely to truncate, showing what most decides the next action, which mission and which step, and whether it is busy. The counts are seen only on hover, which arguably falls short of the goal's statement that the tree lists each mission with its counts of open questions and remaining tasks, and a person cannot compare missions' counts by scanning the list.

A mission's row expands into child rows. The collapsed row carries the title in its label, the next step in its description, and the running marker as a spinning icon. Its children are one row per count, "Open questions" and "Remaining tasks", each with its number in the description, and these children are plain rows with no further children. The tooltip of the mission row repeats all the facts with the path. The counts are shown in full words on rows of their own, never abbreviated or truncated, while the collapsed row still shows the step and whether a run is going. With missions expanded the list is three times as long, and with them collapsed the counts are hidden, so the counts are either costly in space or not visible at a glance. The extension also has to choose and keep a collapsed or expanded default per mission, and the child rows carry information a click on them does nothing with.

A mission's row expands into two child group rows, "Open questions" and "Remaining tasks", each showing its count in its description and expanding in turn into one row per open question title or per remaining task heading, read from the documents the extension already reads. The collapsed mission row carries the title in its label, the next step and both counts in its description, and the running marker as a spinning icon; the tooltip repeats all the facts with the path. The counts are visible both on the collapsed row and on the group rows, and expanding a mission lets a person browse what is open and left without opening its window, which uses the question and task lists the extension already holds. It adds a second view of the questions and tasks beside the mission window's own two panes, beyond what the goal asks the side bar to show, with deeper rows whose clicks need a meaning and whose contents must be kept fresh on every file event. The collapsed row still carries the step and both counts in one description, so it truncates like the one-line leaf.

open-question.question: The side-bar view is a native VS Code tree and must carry the four controls that belong to no mission: New mission, Define mission, Refresh, and Settings. On today's page New mission and Define mission are buttons whose label shows the harness, model, and effort of the variant they run, each with a dropdown beside it that selects among its recipe's variants, and a native tree view holds neither a labelled button nor a dropdown. Where in the side-bar view does each of the four controls sit, and how do New mission and Define mission there show the variant they will run and let a person select another?

Today's mission pane shows the line `No mission is live.` when no mission is live, and one failure state naming the cause when the read of the live missions fails. Once the missions are listed in a native side-bar tree, how does that view show each of those two states, in which it has no mission row to draw?
open-question.alternative: Both states are drawn through the tree view's own `message` property (`TreeView.message`), with the tree returning no rows. With no mission live the message is today's line `No mission is live.`. When the live read fails it is today's failure line `The live missions could not be read.` followed by the cause as the read gave it. A successful read with missions clears the message. Nothing is added to the manifest, and the view's other contents (its title-bar controls included) stay as they are in every state. One dynamic surface serves both states. It sits in the view itself, carries the cause verbatim exactly as the pane's failure state does today, is set and cleared from the same code path that answers each live read, and needs no manifest entry, context key, or extra command, so a stub of the `vscode` module can cover it by recording one property. The message is one plain-text string rendered above the tree, with no Markdown, link, or button. A long or multi-line cause (a Python traceback or git's message) is shown cramped or cut short in a narrow side bar. Neither state offers an action in the body of the view, so with no mission live a person finds New mission and Define mission only where the sibling question on the side-bar controls places them.

Both states are drawn as tree rows that are not missions, returned by the tree data provider in place of mission rows. With no mission live the provider returns one row labelled `No mission is live.`, with no command. When the live read fails it returns one row labelled with the failure line and an error `ThemeIcon`, the cause carried in the row's tooltip and also as non-clickable child rows, one per line of the cause, so expanding the row shows it whole. Each placeholder row carries its own `contextValue`, so no mission menu or click handler applies to it. Everything stays inside the one tree data provider and the one tree. The cause can be shown in full, line by line, however long it is, and can be inspected or copied from the tooltip. No manifest welcome entry, context key, or second rendering mechanism is needed. A placeholder row looks like any other row, so it reads as something to click or expand. Every piece of code that handles rows (the click that opens a mission's window, row menus, the running marker, and the counts) has to tell placeholder rows from mission rows. Any row layout the sibling question on mission rows settles (for example, whether rows expand) has to be kept from leaking into the placeholders. The view also loses VS Code's own empty-view look.

Both states are drawn as `viewsWelcome` content contributed in the manifest for the view. It shows only while the tree has no rows, and the extension picks which entry shows by setting a context key with `setContext` (for example, none live versus read failed). The no-mission entry reads `No mission is live.`. The failure entry reads `The live missions could not be read.`, but its text is static manifest text and cannot hold the cause. So the cause is written to an output channel the extension contributes, and the failure entry carries a command link or button that reveals that channel. Either entry may also carry command links in Markdown, such as Refresh. This is VS Code's native idiom for an empty view. Its Markdown, links, and buttons can put the next action (refreshing, or starting a mission) right in the body of the view, and the extension keeps no extra rows or message text. The cause is no longer in the view itself: a person has to follow a link to an output channel, unlike today's failure state, which names the cause on the page. The approach adds a manifest entry per state, a context key that must be kept true to every read (so the wrong entry never shows, including before the first read lands), an output channel, and a command, and the editor-stub tests cover none of that content. Any button for New mission or Define mission placed in the welcome entries overlaps the axis the sibling question on the side-bar controls owns.

alternative.id: Welcome when none, message on failure

open-question.alternative: Each state gets the surface that fits its content. With no mission live, the view shows `viewsWelcome` content from the manifest, reading `No mission is live.` and optionally carrying command links. When the live read fails, the tree returns no rows and the extension sets `TreeView.message` to the failure line followed by the cause, and it sets a context key that suppresses the welcome entry while the failure stands, so the welcome entry does not also show. A successful read clears both. The fixed state uses the static, native empty-view surface, which can carry actions. The failing state uses the dynamic surface, which carries the cause verbatim in the view as today. Neither state needs placeholder rows or an output channel. Two mechanisms are coordinated by one context key, and a missed update can leave the welcome text and the failure message showing together, or neither. The failure message is still plain text with no link, and long causes are cramped in a narrow side bar. Any welcome-entry button for New mission or Define mission overlaps the axis the sibling question on the side-bar controls owns.

alternative.id: Welcome when none, row on failure

open-question.alternative: With no mission live, the view shows `viewsWelcome` content from the manifest reading `No mission is live.`, optionally with command links. When the live read fails, the tree returns one placeholder row labelled with the failure line and an error `ThemeIcon`, with the cause in its tooltip and as non-clickable child rows, one per line. Because the tree then has a row, the welcome entry is hidden by VS Code itself and needs no context key. The empty state gets the native, action-capable welcome surface, and the failure state shows the full cause, line by line, inside the view. Since a row hides the welcome content, the two states can never show together and no context key needs to be kept in sync. The failure row is a non-mission row, so every row handler (click, menus, running marker, counts) must tell it apart, and it can look clickable. The two states use two different mechanisms. Any welcome-entry button for New mission or Define mission overlaps the axis the sibling question on the side-bar controls owns.

alternative.id: Blank when none, message on failure

open-question.alternative: With no mission live, the view draws nothing: the tree returns no rows, and the extension contributes no welcome content and sets no message, so the line `No mission is live.` is dropped. When the live read fails, the extension sets `TreeView.message` to the failure line followed by the cause, and clears it on the next successful read. This option has the least code and manifest of all. It keeps only the state that tells a person something has gone wrong, names its cause verbatim in the view, and treats an empty list as needing no words. A blank view cannot be told apart from one whose first read has not landed yet or one that failed to draw, and it drops a line the pane shows today. A first-time user also gets no pointer to starting a mission, which is left entirely to wherever the sibling question on the side-bar controls places New mission and Define mission.

open-question.question: When the read of the live missions fails, today's one mission pane replaces every page with a failure state naming the cause. Once each mission has a window of its own in the editor area, what do the mission windows already open show while that read fails?
open-question.alternative: Every open mission window replaces its whole page with the one failure state today's pane draws, the line `The live missions could not be read.` with the cause beneath it, so no mission's diagram, recipes, or panes stay drawn and no action on them can be clicked; each window draws its mission's page again on the next live read that succeeds, and stays open throughout. It carries today's failure state into each window unchanged (the page script's `drawFailure`, the `liveFailure` message, and the rule that no click is accepted against a read that did not succeed), so every surface agrees that nothing is known, and no run can start from a state that may no longer hold. A transient `missions.py live` failure blanks every open window at once, although each mission's `open_questions.xml` and `TASKS_TODO.md` are read in process by `src/documents.ts` and may still read fine, so a person loses the page they were reading for a fault outside their mission; when it recovers depends on the read and watch lifetime the sibling question settles.

Each open mission window keeps the page it last drew, diagram, recipes, preview, and both panes as they stood, with a notice above it naming the cause and saying the page is as of the last successful read; every action button on the page is drawn disabled, as it is today while a run is going, until a live read succeeds and the page is drawn afresh. The person keeps reading the mission's questions and tasks through the fault, while no run can start from a page whose step, state, or very liveness the failed read could not confirm, and the disabled-button drawing already exists for running missions. The page shown may already be wrong, a question answered or a task completed since the last good read, with only the notice to say so, and each window must hold its last drawn state and a separate disabled cause beside the running one, which today's module-level `current` and `posted` do not provide per window.

Each open mission window keeps the page it last drew with a notice above it naming the cause, and its actions stay enabled, so a click runs its recipe against the mission's path as the last successful read gave it. A failure in the live listing, which concerns every mission, stops no work on the mission the person has open: they can still run the review, the sweep, or a task run, and the run itself resolves the mission and stops on its own fixed line if the path no longer holds. Every click is today checked against what the latest answer posted, and here the latest answer is a failure, so the extension must accept clicks against a stale page; a run can start for a mission that has since been finished or whose next step has moved, the person warned only by the notice.

The mission windows change nothing when the live read fails: each keeps the page it last drew, with no notice and its actions as they were, and the failure is shown only where the side-bar view shows it, the windows being redrawn on the next read that succeeds. It needs no failure drawing, per-window state, or message in the mission windows at all, and a short-lived fault never disturbs the page a person is working in. Nothing in the window says its page may be stale or that the extension cannot currently read the missions, so a person working in a window with the side-bar hidden acts on a page the extension no longer vouches for; it rests on the side-bar view showing the failure, which the sibling question on the side-bar view without missions settles.

Each open mission window stops relying on the failed live read for its content: it re-reads its own mission's `open_questions.xml` and `TASKS_TODO.md` in process, as `src/documents.ts` already does apart from `missions.py live`, and draws the panes from that fresh read, each with its own notice where its file is missing or does not parse, while the workflow diagram shows no step to run next, since `nextStep` needs the started or defined state only the live read gives; a notice names the cause, and every action button is drawn disabled until a live read succeeds. The panes stay current through the fault, a question answered or a task completed still showing, because the documents do not depend on the read that failed, while no run starts without the state the step choice needs. A window reads its mission's files apart from any confirmation that the mission is still live, so a directory removed by finishing reads as missing files rather than an ended mission, and the window must draw a partial page (panes without a step) that no state of today's page has; its reads depend on the watching that the read and watch lifetime question settles.

Each open mission window re-reads its own mission's `open_questions.xml` and `TASKS_TODO.md` in process and draws the panes from that fresh read, the diagram showing no step to run next, with a notice naming the cause, and its recipes and action buttons stay enabled, a click running against the mission's path as the last successful read gave it. Work on the open mission goes on with current panes through a fault in the listing of every mission, and the run, which resolves its mission itself, refuses a path that no longer holds on its own fixed line. Actions are offered with no step to run next and against a liveness and state the extension could not confirm, so clicks must be accepted against a failed answer and a person picks a recipe without the diagram's guidance, while the window also carries the partial-page drawing and the unconfirmed-liveness reads of the option above.

Every open mission window is closed when the live read fails, and a person opens a mission again from the side-bar view once a read succeeds and lists it. No window can show or act on a state the extension cannot confirm, and the windows need no failure drawing of their own, the failure standing only in the side-bar view. A transient fault throws away every open window, with its scroll position, selected pane, and question view position, and the person must reopen each by hand; it also treats a mission whose liveness is merely unknown as the windows of ended missions are treated, a case the sibling question on the window of an ended mission settles separately.

open-question.question: Each mission's row in the side-bar tree shows the workflow step to run next and the counts of open questions and remaining tasks. The extension finds no next step when a read that choice needs failed, and holds a notice in place of a list when a mission's `open_questions.xml` or `TASKS_TODO.md` is missing or does not parse. What does a mission's row show in place of a step or a count that could not be read?
open-question.alternative: The row draws only the facts that read. A step or count that could not be read is left off the row with nothing in its place: no placeholder, no marker, and no cause on the row. The cause is shown only where the mission's page already shows it, the notice of the file that did not read in place of its list, once the mission's window is opened. It adds nothing to the tree. The row needs no new text, the extension gets no new state to draw, and the page's existing notice stays the one place a failed read is explained. A failure reads as an absence. A row with no step looks like a mission with nothing to do, and a row with a missing count can be mistaken for one with no questions or no tasks unless a zero is always drawn. A failed git read, which today leaves the diagram with no filled block and no notice anywhere, is then explained nowhere. Whether an absence can be seen at all depends on how the sibling question Mission row layout places the facts on the row.

Each step or count that could not be read is replaced, on its own, by one fixed placeholder (such as `?`) in the slot where its value would stand, and the facts that did read are drawn as usual. The row carries no cause. The cause is left to the mission's window, where the page's notice names the file and whether it is missing or does not parse. The row's shape stays the same whatever reads, so an unread fact cannot be mistaken for a zero count or for no next step. It costs one fixed string and no new detail to compose. The row says that something failed but not what, so a person has to open the window to learn the cause, and a failed git read, the step's other cause, has no notice on the page to point to. A single character can be overlooked in a long list of missions.

Each step or count that could not be read is replaced, on its own, by one fixed placeholder in its slot, the facts that did read drawn as usual. The row's hover text names the cause of each unread fact: the file that is missing or does not parse, with its path, or for the step a failed git read. The row gets no warning icon or colour. The cause can be read from the side-bar without opening anything, the failed git read included, which the page explains nowhere today. Each fact still degrades on its own, so the counts that did read stay visible. The hover text now carries a failure detail beside whatever the sibling question Mission row layout assigns to it, and the extension has to compose a cause for the step, which `nextStep` today reports only as undefined. Without a marker the failure is noticed only by someone who spots the placeholder.

Each step or count that could not be read is replaced, on its own, by one fixed placeholder in its slot, the facts that did read drawn as usual. The row's hover text names the cause of each unread fact (the file and whether it is missing or does not parse, or a failed git read), and the row as a whole carries a warning mark, such as a warning icon or a warning colour, while any of its facts could not be read. A failure is seen at a glance across every live mission and explained on hover, while the facts that did read stay on the row. The mark takes a slot of the row that the sibling question Mission row layout may already give to the running marker or to the step, so its viability depends on that assignment, and a mark and a running marker on one row have to be told apart. It is the most added text and state of the options.

When any of the step and the two counts could not be read, the row draws none of the three. It shows one fixed failure word (such as `unreadable`) in their place, with a warning mark, and its hover text names every cause. A row whose facts all read is drawn as usual. One fixed state per row, the same whatever failed, matching the one failure state today's pane draws for a failed read. Because a failed question document or task list often leaves the step unchosen too, the row seldom has much left to show anyway. It hides facts that did read, such as the open-question count while only the task list fails, which still yields a step. The warning mark depends on the slot the sibling question Mission row layout leaves free.

Each step or count that could not be read is replaced, on its own, by a short text of its cause written in the slot itself, such as `TASKS_TODO.md missing`, `open_questions.xml does not parse`, or `git read failed`, the facts that did read drawn as usual. No separate hover detail or warning mark is added for it. The cause can be read on the row itself without hovering or opening anything, and nothing beyond the row's own text is needed. The cause text is far longer than a count, so a native tree row, which cuts off long text, may show a mangled or partly hidden cause and push the title or the other facts out of view. How much room there is depends on the slots the sibling question Mission row layout gives each fact.

open-question.question: Each mission opens in a window of its own in the editor area, several at once beside the Settings window, and an editor tab shows a title and optionally an icon. Today's tab row shows each mission's title with its path as a tooltip, and two missions in different scopes may carry the same title. What does a mission window's editor tab show so that several open missions can be told apart?
A mission's window can still be open when its mission stops being live, as when finishing the mission removes its directory. What happens to that window then?
open-question.alternative: The extension disposes the mission's window as soon as a live read no longer lists its path, with no notification, whether or not a run of that mission is still going. The window is the mission's, so it ends with the mission. The simplest rule, and it keeps the editor area in step with the side-bar tree: every open mission window belongs to a live mission, so no window ever needs a state for a mission that is gone. Finishing is usually started from the mission's own window, so the window that launched the finish run closes while that run's terminal is still showing, and the person is not told why it went beyond the mission's row leaving the side-bar. A branch switch or a hand rename that only hides a mission for a moment closes its window too.

The extension disposes the mission's window as soon as a live read no longer lists its path, and shows one VS Code information notification naming the mission and saying it is no longer live, whether or not a run of that mission is still going. Keeps every open window tied to a live mission, as closing at once does, while telling the person why a window they may have been looking at disappeared. Adds a notification on every finish, the expected outcome of the workflow, and on every branch switch that hides a mission, which is noise once the person knows the rule; the finish run's own window still closes under its running terminal.

A mission window whose mission is no longer live closes silently, at once when no run of that mission is going and otherwise when that run stops being noted as running (its terminal dismissed, as `RunningRuns` notes it today), its page meanwhile staying as last drawn with every action disabled as during any run. A finish run ends with its own window still standing beside its terminal until the person is done with it, and the editor area is still left holding only live missions' windows afterwards. Ties the window's lifetime to the run bookkeeping in `src/runs.ts`, one more listener path to keep right and test against the stubbed `vscode` module; a mission that vanished with no run going still closes with no word.

The window stays open and replaces the mission's page with one fixed notice that the mission is no longer live, drawing no workflow diagram, recipe, pane, or action button; the person closes it. If a later live read lists the path again (a reverted finish, a branch switched back), the window draws that mission's page again. Nothing disappears under the person: the outcome is stated in the place they were looking, no action can be started against a directory that is gone, and a mission that comes back simply returns to its own window. Ended windows pile up in the editor area until closed by hand, and the extension must keep tracking a path no live read lists, so a window can exist with no side-bar row behind it.

The window stays open and replaces the mission's page with a notice that the mission is no longer live, beneath which, when the bundled `missions.py summary` reads the mission as finished, it shows the finish date and the summary bullets of its `Mission-finish:` commit, and otherwise the bare notice; no action button is drawn and the person closes it. If a later live read lists the path again, the window draws that mission's page again. Turns the end of a mission into a readable close: the person sees what the finished mission recorded, read through the tool that already holds that record, rather than a blank state. Adds a read the extension makes nowhere today (`summary` against git history), a second content shape to draw and test, and a failure path of its own when that read fails; the piling up of ended windows and the tracking of a non-live path remain.

The window stays open and replaces the mission's page with one fixed notice that the mission is no longer live, with no action button, and is detached for good: if the path is listed live again later, this window keeps the notice and the person opens the mission afresh from the side-bar. A window's binding to its mission changes only one way, so the extension forgets an ended mission at once and never has to reconcile a stale window with a mission that reappeared. After a reverted finish or a branch switched back, the person is left with a dead window beside the live mission and must close one and open another, and two windows standing for one path can confuse.

The window stays open showing the mission's page exactly as last drawn, its diagram, recipes, and panes unchanged but every action button disabled, under a note that the mission is no longer live; the person closes it. If a later live read lists the path again, the page is redrawn live. The person keeps the last view of the mission's questions and tasks to read after it ended, which a bare notice throws away, with no new read needed to show it. A page drawn for a directory that no longer exists can be mistaken for a live one if the note is missed, and keeping it means holding the last-read mission state per window past the mission's life; ended windows pile up as with any window that stays.

Nothing is done for the ended mission's window: it keeps whatever it last drew, its buttons still enabled, and any click on them is refused by the check of every click against the latest read that exists today; it redraws if the path is listed live again. No new state, notice, or lifecycle rule to build or test; the existing click check already prevents a run against a mission that is gone. The window looks fully live while it is not, every click on it fails, and the person learns the mission ended only by a refusal or by noticing its row left the side-bar.

open-question.question: The extension registers no `WebviewPanelSerializer`, so today's one mission pane does not survive a restart or a window reload and is opened again by its command. Once missions and Settings open in windows of their own from a side-bar view that VS Code restores by itself, do the mission windows and the Settings window that were open come back after a restart or reload, or does a person open them again from the side-bar?
open-question.alternative: Both the mission windows and the Settings window that were open come back after a restart or a window reload, in the editor group and tab position they held. The extension registers a `WebviewPanelSerializer` for the mission window's view type and one for the Settings window's, and adds an `onWebviewPanel:` activation event for each to the manifest beside its present command activation. Each mission window keeps its mission's path in its webview state, so on restore it is redrawn from a fresh read of the live missions for that path, and the page's own `setState` values (such as each question view's position) come back with it; the Settings window is redrawn from the harness states, lists, variants, and single-task lines read afresh, as each opening reads them today. The working layout a person built, several missions open side by side beside Settings, survives every reload exactly as left, so a reload (frequent while the extension itself is being developed, and after every install of a new VSIX) costs no clicks, and the editor's own restore mechanism places every window where it was. It reverses the first version's recorded no-serializer decision and adds two deserialize paths, two activation events, and per-window state the pane tests' `vscode` stub does not stand in for; the extension now activates at startup whenever such a window was open, and a restored window can name a mission that finished, or a path that no longer matches, while the window was closed, so its viability depends on how the window-of-ended-mission question is settled, and restoring Settings may trigger the harness check at startup depending on how the harness-check-lifetime question is settled.

The mission windows that were open come back after a restart or a window reload, through a `WebviewPanelSerializer` for the mission window's view type and its `onWebviewPanel:` activation event, each keeping its mission's path in its webview state, redrawn from a fresh read for that path, with the page's own `setState` values restored. The Settings window does not come back: it is closed by the reload, as today's pane is, and a person opens it again from the side-bar view or from any mission window. It keeps the part of the layout that is a person's ongoing work, the missions they had open, while treating Settings as the occasional, transient view it is, so no harness check, variant read, or harness-state read runs at startup on behalf of a window nobody asked for again, and only one deserialize path is added. It still reverses the recorded no-serializer decision and carries the same activation, state, and test-stub cost for mission windows, and a restored window can name a mission that finished while the window was closed (its viability depending on how the window-of-ended-mission question is settled); a person who kept Settings open across a reload, for instance while editing variants, has to reopen it each time, and the two kinds of window behave differently on reload, which has to be explained.

Neither the mission windows nor the Settings window come back after a restart or a window reload: no `WebviewPanelSerializer` is registered, as today, so the editor drops every such window on reload, and a person opens each one again from the side-bar view, which the editor restores by itself, or Settings from a mission window. This is the direction of not restoring now; a serializer may still be added by a later mission. It keeps the first version's recorded no-serializer decision and adds no deserialize path, activation event, or per-window state to build and test, the extension never activates at startup on behalf of a window, and a window for a mission that finished while the editor was closed can never come back, since every window is opened from the side-bar's fresh list of live missions. The cost of a reload grows with the new shape: where today one command reopens one pane holding every mission, a person who had several mission windows and Settings open must find and click each again, losing the layout and the page's saved positions every time, which is most felt during the extension's own development and after each VSIX install.

open-question.question: The extension contributes two commands today: `gurita.openMissionPane` (Gurita: Open Mission Pane), its only entry point, and `gurita.refreshMissionPane`. Once the activity-bar view is the entry point and the one mission pane no longer exists, which commands does the extension offer in the Command Palette, and do the two existing ones stay, change, or go?

Today the extension reads the live missions and watches the mission files only while the mission pane exists, and while the pane is hidden a file event only marks it stale until it is shown again. With a side-bar tree listing every live mission and several mission windows open at once, from when until when does the extension read the missions and watch their files, and is a hidden side-bar view or a hidden window re-read on a file event or only once it is shown again?

Today a click on a mission's tab in the pane also brings that mission's run terminal forward. With the tab row gone, does any action in the side-bar tree or on a mission's window still bring that mission's run terminal forward, and which?

The harness check runs the first time the settings view is opened after the mission pane's panel is created, and its result is kept for that panel's lifetime and run again only by the check-again control. Once Settings is a window of its own and no single mission pane exists, when does the check first run, and for how long is its result kept before it runs again by itself?

The activity-bar icon is generated by a script from the README banner's drawing as three of its arms, a large one in the centre and a smaller one on each side. `assets/banner.txt` holds eight arms, all drawn at one character scale, a shorter and a longer kind whose heights differ by two of ten rows, and no drawing of three arms or of an arm at a larger scale exists. Which three of the eight arms does the script take, and how does the centre arm come to be larger than the two beside it?

The banner's SVG draws each character of the drawing as text in a system monospace font, in three colours, on a grid of 10 by 20 pixels per cell. The editor shows an activity-bar icon at 24 by 24 pixels in one fill colour. In what form does the icon script draw the three arms in the icon's SVG, and how much of each arm's detail (its brackets, suckers, and curl) does the icon keep at that size?

The banner's SVG is a tracked file regenerated by hand with `scripts/render_banner.py`, a stdlib-only Python script, and pinned to that script's output by `tests/test_banner.py`. The extension's other generated files are written into the git-ignored `gurita-vscode/bundled/` by the Node script `gurita-vscode/scripts/bundle.js` at every package. Where does the script that generates the activity-bar icon live and in which language, is the icon it writes a tracked file or a package-time output, and does a test pin the icon to the script's output?

The mission removes `ideas/vscode_extension.md`. `ideas/vscode_extension_follow_up.md` names that file in its opening as the design the first version was built from and cites it throughout as the draft. What happens to those references once the draft is removed?

The mission removes `ideas/vscode_extension.md`, whose section What was checked of VS Code is the repository's only record of the webview-panel facts read from the editor's documentation. Does that record move into another file before the draft is removed, and into which, or does it leave the tree with the draft and stay only in git history?
